title: The Agentic Scientist – SakanaAI
content:
Turn a task description into experiments, ablations, and a paper, driven by coding agents.
Agentic Scientist treats coding agents as AI scientists. Starting from a
task.md, the agents propose ideas, run experiments, evaluate outcomes against
the task rubric, and iterate toward stronger programs. The pipeline then runs
baselines and ablations, a sealed final evaluation, post-hoc analyses, and
writes the paper, with every stage kept under one run directory.
The recommended setup runs every agent phase inside Docker, which is the
default for agsci run. Install Docker,
then build the agent image:
docker build -t agentic-scientist/agent-cli:latest -f src/docker/agent-cli/Dockerfile .
If the build cannot reach package mirrors, add --network=host to the
docker build command.
Security note — Agentic Scientist launches coding agents with full tool
permissions (Headless --allow yolo). They can run arbitrary commands and
inherit the API keys you give them, and the task files and papers they read
steer what they do. Keep runs inside the Docker image rather than on your
workstation, only run tasks and sources you trust, and review run directories
before sharing them: agent logs can echo document contents and paths.
- Python ≥ 3.11 with uv. uv sync creates .venv and installs the agsci command:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh uv sync source .venv/bin/activate
- API keys in a .env file at the repo root (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, ... whichever your agent
needs). The pipeline mounts it into the agent containers. Never commit it.
- Agent CLIs are already inside the image. For native (non-containerized) runs, install the CLI of the agent you use plus Git and Node.js; versions and commands are in docs/install.md.
- GPUs are required only by the GPU task presets. The pipeline discovers
them through nvidia-smi and refuses to start compute phases unless the
visible GPUs match the preset.
- Autoillustrate (optional) is built into the image for concept figures. To use it directly on the host, follow the single-command install in the Autoillustrate README.
Run agsci doctor to check the host, or agsci doctor examples/<task> preset=<task>
to check everything one specific run needs (CLI, credentials, image, GPUs, task
scaffold).
Point agsci run at a task directory. This runs the default six phases
(task drafting → investigation → ablations → final evaluation → post-hoc analysis
→ paper) on the CPU-only circle-packing example:
agsci run examples/circpack
Add --dry-run to validate the configuration and preview the exact commands
without running anything. Every option is a Hydra key=value override; agsci run --help lists them all.
Note — Agentic Scientist drives claude, codex, cursor, opencode,
gemini, and pi through
Headless CLI, so the same
experiment can be repeated across agents and models: pick one with
agent.name=<agent> agent.model=<model>.
Task drafting only writes a scaffold when the task directory has none; every shipped example already includes its evaluator, so the drafting phase only snapshots it and the investigation phase builds and validates the task runtime. Drafting a task from a bare research brief is experimental (see example 8).
Each run writes one predictable envelope under results/:
results/<task>/<agent>/<run_id>/
├── task_drafting/ # drafting logs and validation audit
├── task/          # immutable run-local task snapshot
├── investigation/  # ideas, attempts, winner, and optimizer memory
├── ablations/     # baselines and ablations
├── final_evaluation/         # sealed final evaluation
├── posthoc/       # post-hoc analyses
└── paper/         # manuscript, PDF, manifest, and optional AI reviews
Investigation plus the task snapshot is enough to write a paper; the other
phases add evidence when available and are reported as degraded when they fail.
Browse any run in the browser with agsci inspect start
(http://127.0.0.1:8765).
The default configuration is the one to start with: the claude agent, every
phase in Docker, and the CPU-only examples/circpack task. It needs a Claude
login, no GPUs, and exercises every phase through to a compiled paper.
- Build the image and the Python environment as described in Install.
- Create .env at the repo root. Only the selected agent's keys are
forwarded into its containers:
CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN=... # claude, billed to your Claude subscription (ANTHROPIC_API_KEY for pay-per-token) OPENAI_API_KEY=... # recommended: concept figures in the paper and the `review` phase Other agents: codex reads OPENAI_API_KEY or CODEX_API_KEY, gemini reads GEMINI_API_KEY, cursor reads CURSOR_API_KEY, and Bedrock-backed
Claude reads the AWS_* variables. Concept figures use OPENAI_API_KEY,
fall back to GEMINI_API_KEY, and otherwise ship a plain export.
- Export host variables only if you need them. Everything else (host
networking, the image, the .env mount) is already the agsci run default:
export AGENTIC_TEMP_ROOT=/path/to/scratch # existing writable dir on a large disk; default: $TMPDIR, /mnt/localssd, or /tmp export AGENT_CONTAINER_GPUS=device=<UUID,...> # GPU presets only: which GPUs to use; default: the first `container.gpu_count` (x investigation workers) from nvidia-smi
- Check, preview, then run. Shrinking the ablation and post-hoc budgets makes the first end-to-end run finish faster without skipping a phase: agsci doctor examples/circpack # host, image, credentials, task scaffold agsci run examples/circpack --dry-run # print every phase command, run nothing agsci run examples/circpack \ investigation.execution.max_idea_cycles=2 \ ablations.execution.num_replications=1 \ ablations.execution.max_evals_per_variant=2 \ posthoc.execution.max_selected_analyses=1 The paper lands in results/circpack/claude/<run_id>/paper/paper.pdf; agsci inspect start browses the run. Drop the overrides for the default
budgets (3 idea cycles, 5 ablation replications, 3 post-hoc analyses), then
move on to the GPU task preset and a pinned model, for example agsci run examples/grpo preset=grpo agent.model=claude-sonnet-5.
Task presets under configs/preset/ hold the campaign budgets, timeouts,
paper format, and required GPUs. configs/preset/paper.yaml is the shared
campaign preset and configs/preset/grpo.yaml composes it for the GRPO task
(two GPUs, harness-side GPU evaluation):
agsci run examples/grpo preset=grpo
Explicit overrides win over the preset:
agsci run examples/grpo preset=grpo \
  agent.name=opencode \
  agent.model=amazon-bedrock/global.anthropic.claude-opus-5-5 \
  investigation.execution.max_idea_cycles=20
Every phase resumes against the run directory. The pipeline recovers the original idea-cycle budget; pass the original agent and model again:
# Continue after investigation with ablations, post-hoc analysis, and the paper:
agsci run examples/circpack execution.phases=ablations,posthoc,paper \
  paths.run_dir=results/circpack/claude/20260331_094917
# Rewrite only the paper:
agsci run examples/circpack execution.phases=paper \
  paths.run_dir=results/circpack/claude/20260331_094917
Adding the review phase sends the complete manuscript to the OpenAI-backed
reviewer. Review failures are recorded but never discard the paper:
agsci run examples/circpack paper.paper_format=iclr \
  execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,ablations,final_evaluation,posthoc,paper,review
The same reviewer runs standalone on any PDF with agsci review. It reads
OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment or the repo .env and prints the review
JSON:
agsci review results/circpack/claude/<run_id>/paper/paper.pdf --output review.json
Each phase composes its stage's own config, so any stage key is reachable as
<phase>.<key>:
agsci run examples/circpack \
  investigation.execution.max_idea_cycles=5 \
  ablations.execution.num_replications=1 \
  posthoc.execution.max_selected_analyses=2 \
  paper.paper_format=iclr paper.paper_review_rounds=1
agsci investigate (src/investigation/cli.py) runs the idea/experiment loop on its own, natively by d

report.summary: Sakana AI's Agentic Scientist turns a task description into autonomous experiments, ablations, sealed evaluations, and a compiled research paper using headless coding agents.
report.background: Sakana AI has iterated on the 'AI Scientist' concept since 2024, when its first pipeline showed an LLM could generate ideas, run code, and write papers end-to-end. Those early versions relied heavily on single-model prompting and scripted loops, which produced shallow experiments and hard-to-verify results. Agentic Scientist (AI-Scientist-v3) reflects the industry's shift toward coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, opencode, Gemini CLI, and pi — tools that can read files, install packages, and iterate on real codebases. That capability makes the loop closer to actual scientific practice: hypothesize, implement, measure, ablate, and report. It also raises unresolved questions about reproducibility, evaluation rigor, prompt-injection risk, and whether AI-generated manuscripts can meet peer-review standards, which the project addresses with sealed final evaluations, task rubrics, and per-run artifacts.
key_points: The pipeline runs six phases from a single task directory: task drafting, investigation, ablations, final evaluation, post-hoc analysis, and paper writing. Starting from task.md, agents propose ideas, run experiments, score results against the task rubric, and iterate toward stronger programs before baselines and ablations are executed.

It is deliberately model-agnostic. Agentic Scientist drives claude, codex, cursor, opencode, gemini, and pi through their headless CLIs, so the same experiment can be repeated across different agents and models via agent.name=<agent> agent.model=<model>, making cross-agent comparisons straightforward.

Everything lands in one predictable run envelope under results/<task>/<agent>/<run_id>/, with separate folders for investigation memory, ablations, sealed evaluation, post-hoc work, and the manuscript. Phases resume against that directory, and agsci inspect start browses any run in a browser.

Security is an explicit design concern. Agents launch with full tool permissions in what the docs call 'headless --allow yolo' mode, can run arbitrary commands, and inherit injected API keys. The documentation warns that task files and papers steer agent behavior, so runs should stay inside Docker and only trusted inputs should be used.

Configuration is Hydra-based key=value overrides, with presets for budgets, timeouts, paper format, and GPU requirements. agsci doctor validates the host, credentials, image, and GPUs, while --dry-run previews commands without executing them, and the CPU-only circle-packing example exercises every phase.

The project is candid about limits. Drafting a task from a bare research brief is labeled experimental, failed ablations or post-hoc phases are reported as degraded rather than fatal, and the paper can still be produced from investigation plus the task snapshot alone.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Agentic Scientist pushes autonomous research from demo to infrastructure, normalizing agent-orchestrated experiments, sealed evaluation, and cross-model benchmarking. For developers, it offers a concrete template for wrapping coding agents in resumable, containerized, phase-based pipelines — Docker isolation, Hydra configs, run directories, and a CLI discipline that many agent projects lack. For regular users, the near-term effect is more AI-written papers and benchmarks appearing online, which raises the bar on verification: readers will need to check rubrics, ablations, and run artifacts rather than trusting abstracts. The larger risk is an arms race in volume over rigor, and the larger opportunity is cheaper, faster exploration of narrow, well-specified empirical questions.
report.tools: Watch Sakana AI's AI-Scientist-v3 and its predecessors (AI-Scientist, AI-Scientist-v2) for the evolving reference implementation, plus its optional Autoillustrate module for concept figures. Practical companions: Docker for sandboxed agent runs, uv for Python environments, Hydra for configuration, and the headless CLIs of Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, opencode, and Gemini. For evaluation, look at agsci review and paper formats like ICLR, and compare against open agent-research frameworks such as Agent Laboratory.
